The two steps are not redundant: k1 tests rationalization in isolation on a prime radicand (9 is a genuine coefficient, no simplification step exists for √5); ch1 tests the INTEGRATION of simplify-then-rationalize on a composite radicand (27), which is strictly more work and combines skills k1 alone never exercises. (k2, which is structurally closest to ch1's 2-step pipeline, is correctly left unflagged, since it is ch1's actual technique-donor, not a duplicate of it.) KEPT as authored; no file changes made.

rationale: PROGRESSION [k1]: i1 ('what is f(49)?', numeric widget) and k1 ('what is f(9)?', mcq widget) both share the 'what is f(N)?' evaluation template, but they test different failure modes by design. i1 is pure computation fluency: its commonErrors catch ARITHMETIC slips (halving instead of rooting: 24.5; squaring instead of rooting: 2401) — a numeric-input widget can only catch wrong-operation errors, not a belief in multiple answers. k1, body 'The principal root.', is the lesson's first formal check of its actual conceptual thesis (c2: '√ symbol means the principal, nonnegative root') — its MCQ options deliberately surface the ± TEMPTATION as selectable distractors ('±3', '−3'), a misconception check that is structurally impossible to build with a bare numeric-input widget (there is no way to 'enter ±3' or 'enter the wrong sign' as a typed number the way there is to select it from a list). The widget-type change (numeric -> mcq) is not incidental; it is what makes the ± misconception representable at all. KEPT as authored; no file changes made.

rationale: PROGRESSION [i2,k3]: k1, i2, and k3 all share the surface template 'How many real solutions does x^(p/q) = k have?' (mcq), which the normalizer flags as repeats. But the three are an explicit, deliberately-labeled 3-way contrast covering the complete case analysis this lesson exists to teach: k1 (body 'Count the solutions.') is EVEN numerator (2/5) with a POSITIVE target (4) -> TWO solutions (±32). i2's body is literally labeled 'Odd numerator control case' -- an explicit authorial tell that this step is a deliberate CONTROL for k1, not a repeat of it: ODD numerator (3/5), same-shape positive target (8) -> exactly ONE solution (32), directly falsifying the naive over-generalization 'even-numerator behavior applies to all rational exponents.' k3's body is 'A negative target.': EVEN numerator (2/3) again, but now a NEGATIVE target (−4) -> ZERO solutions, since (∛x)² can never be negative -- the third distinct outcome category. Each of the three steps yields a DIFFERENT solution count (2, 1, 0) driven by a genuinely different structural condition (numerator parity x target sign), which is the entire content of this lesson's recap ('Even numerator: two real solutions... Odd numerator: exactly one... Even-numerator powers can never equal a negative: no solution'). This is compare-and-contrast pedagogy, not duplication. KEPT as authored; no file changes made.
reopenCondition: If a reviewer wants the fourth logical case (odd numerator, negative target -> always exactly one negative solution) added as an explicit fourth check, since it is not currently tested anywhere in the lesson.

Grade-1 appropriate: both steps reuse the exact same simple sentence frame, changing only which named shape is being retrieved. KEPT as authored; no file changes made.

rationale: PROGRESSION [k1,i2,i3,k2,k3,ch1]: all seven clockSet steps in this lesson (i1=4:00 [unflagged, first occurrence], k1=6:30, i2=8:00, i3=2:30, k2=1:00, k3=10:30, ch1=12:00) collapse to the identical text skeleton 'Set the clock to show H:MM.' under digit-normalization, because the normalizer strips the minute digits (00/30) exactly as it strips the hour digits -- it cannot see the ON-THE-HOUR-VS-HALF-PAST distinction at all, which is precisely and explicitly this lesson's entire subject (title: 'On the Hour or Half Past?'; c1: 'Check the minute hand first... Then read the hour'). Examining the actual sequence: minute value alternates PERFECTLY every single step -- :00, :30, :00, :30, :00, :30, :00 -- across i1 through ch1. A seven-step perfect alternation is not incidental; it is the deliberate discrimination-practice structure the lesson concept text describes (c3: 'Mixing up which hand tells the hour is a common slip'), forcing the student to re-check the minute hand's position fresh on every single step rather than anchoring on the previous step's mode. Hour values (4,6,8,2,1,10,12) also cover 7 of 12 clock positions with zero repeats, and ch1 (12:00) lands on the lesson's hardest discrimination case: both hands AT 12 simultaneously (distinguished from a half-past reading where the hour hand would sit between 11 and 12). This is compare-and-contrast pedagogy by design, invisible to a detector that discards all digits including the very digit (the minute value) the lesson is built around. KEPT as authored; no file changes made.
